cur:manuscripts-valcavado-sixth-seal.summary: In a starry blue medallion at the top, the Lord sits enthroned between angels and standing elders; below, the sun and moon are darkened, stars fall, and in the lowest register the people of the earth hide in caves and among the mountains.
facts: The Valcavado Beatus was written and illuminated in 970 by the monk Oveco for Abbot Sempronius of Valcavado, in the reign of Ramiro III of León; it has 230 surviving leaves and 87 miniatures.
After the expulsion of the Jesuits under Charles III, the manuscript passed from their college of San Ambrosio in Valladolid to the University of Valladolid.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-115-cruci.summary: Above, Christ hangs on the cross, beardless and nimbed and wearing the long colobium, with the titulus and a wreath above his head and the Virgin and John to the right. To the left the psalmist, freed from his bonds and clad only in a loincloth, holds the 'cup of salvation' to receive the blood from Christ's side, and a paten with the host, while a figure perhaps meant as Longinus approaches from below. Before the Lord's house saints are martyred: 'precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints'. It is one of the earliest images of Christ's blood received in a chalice.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
The psalter was made in or near Reims, probably under Archbishop Ebbo (816–835); some scholars argue for a date around 850 under his successor Hincmar.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-115-cruci.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server. This folio carries two drawings; the crop shows the one for this text.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-140-chris.summary: In a tabernacle whose doors are held open by angels, the psalmist swings a censer before the altar, and the incense rises to the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos, who leans from heaven with three angels and a cross-staff to receive it: 'let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense'. The moon and stars mark the evening sacrifice, while below demons tie up a net full of sinners. This psalm was sung at Vespers.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
After centuries in England the manuscript arrived in Utrecht in 1716; it is often called the most valuable manuscript in the Netherlands.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-140-chris.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:monumental-tokali-entry.summary: In a narrative frieze against a blue ground, Christ, haloed and inscribed IC XC, rides a white donkey towards the gate of a city at the right, where a crowd waits, while a figure in a tree above watches and another spreads a garment before him. The strip-like composition with Greek captions is typical of the long Gospel cycles of Cappadocian churches.
facts: Tokalı Kilise ('Church of the Buckle'), the largest church at Göreme, comprises an Old Church of the 10th century, painted in strips of red and green, and a larger New Church of the late 10th or early 11th century whose walls are dominated by rich indigo blue made from lapis lazuli.
The scene is captioned BAIOPHOROS, the Greek name of the Palm Sunday feast; the figure in the tree cutting branches follows Matthew 21:8.

cur:monumental-tokali-entry.notes: Some have read the figure in the tree as Zacchaeus and the scene as Christ entering Jericho, but the Greek caption BAIOPHOROS (Palm Sunday), visible in the companion photograph of this frieze, confirms the Entry into Jerusalem. The photograph shows a detail of the wall; whether the scene belongs to the Old or the New Church is not stated in the source. Dates for both phases are debated (c. 910s–920s for the Old Church; mid-10th to early 11th century for the New).

cur:objects-sinai-saint-peter-icon.summary: The apostle Peter stands in a gold halo, holding the keys of the Kingdom and a staff topped by a cross, his weathered face turned slightly toward the viewer. Above him, in three medallions, appear Christ at the centre with the Virgin and St John at the sides. The arrangement, recalling the portraits of officials on consular diptychs, presents Peter as the servant of the Lord who presides over him from heaven.
facts: Wikipedia describes it as a sixth-century encaustic icon, one of the oldest surviving icons of St Peter; above his head is a Deesis-like row of half-figures in medallions with Christ, the Virgin and John the Evangelist.
It survived Iconoclasm because Saint Catherine's Monastery lay outside the reach of the iconoclast emperors (context of the Sinai icons).
cur:objects-sinai-saint-peter-icon.notes: Dated 6th century by Wikipedia; the Commons file metadata gives 7th century.

walters:36.12.summary: The Virgin holds the Christ Child, who reaches up to touch his mother's chin in a tender gesture, while the archangels Michael and Gabriel stand guard with drawn swords; the facing panel shows rows of apostles and a mounted saint. The diptych is attributed to a follower of Fre Seyon, the monk-painter of Emperor Zara Yaqob's reign who is the first Ethiopian artist known by name. His oval faces, large almond eyes and bold, flat colour shaped Ethiopian icon painting for generations.
facts: Emperor Zara Yaqob (r. 1434–1468), deeply devoted to the Virgin, instituted thirty-two Marian feasts and encouraged the making of Marian hymns and icons.
The Child's gesture of touching his mother's chin was probably inspired by 15th-century Italian paintings then greatly admired at the Ethiopian royal court.
Fre Seyon's name, meaning 'Fruit of Zion', is known from a single signed icon at the monastery of Daga Estifanos on Lake Tana, making him the earliest identified Ethiopian painter.
Mounted warrior saints had great appeal for Ethiopia's upper classes, whose noblemen were trained in horsemanship and combat.
